article.title: ¡No Pasaran! - YDSA
article.content: Keeping Nazis Off Your Campus Rain drizzled softly onto Red Square as five comrades filled the air with cigarette smoke. We laughed and discussed theory with a rotating cast of excited students who joined us for brief stints on watch between classes. Lively debates spilled over from last night’s open assembly. The tense air that had hung over campus the day before had dissipated, replaced by renewed confidence. If any Nazis decided to show their faces again, they’d be driven out. Those of us who were active under the first Trump presidency or who took part in certain Palestine Solidarity Encampments are veterans of a bloody street war between socialists and fascists. A war that the left ultimately won, even if we tend to forget that. However, despite past victories we must not become complacent. In recent years, the struggle against fascism has largely shifted to confronting state power, rather than groups on the street — but the return of organized fascist street presence is not out of the realm of possibility. There have already been attempts by the far-right to reignite street conflict (though pathetic so far), and I am certain for some readers, the struggle never really died down. No matter the size of your town, it’s always smart to prepare: even tiny mountain towns have spontaneously taken center stage in the national anti-fascist struggle. Everything Starts With A Small Group Red Rabbits graphic from DSA’s Democratic Left newspaper in 2020. While each chapter’s Red Rabbits working group looks different, they typically focus on street medicine, protest safety, and community self-defence. Being prepared means planning ahead of time. If your chapter doesn’t already have one, consider forming a Red Rabbits working group. Gather people willing and able to take the time to learn the skills and take the risks necessary to defend your community. Educate yourselves on de-escalation, self-defense, local law and protest medicine. Reach out to off-campus groups that have experience in anti-fascist action, put up flyers on local fascist activity, research similar situations and teach the public the skills you have learned. As your cadre grows in strength, it’s important to remain grounded in your larger chapter and community. Street groups risk becoming detached from the people they claim to defend. Remember, you aren’t a romantic warrior band — you are socialists, and socialists understand that only the masses can make history, not small cliques (no matter how dedicated they are). Our hastily-put-together “open assembly” flyer which we distributed across campus. We gathered over 40 participants for an effective discussion, putting together both short and long-term plans. Once right-wingers begin to harass your campus, people will begin to take independent action against them, which is good. However, if these disparate plans aren’t composed into something synergetic, contradictions between actions can end up being messily hashed out on the ground rather than in a shared planning space, hurting the whole movement. It’s good to get people talking to each other as soon as possible, and an open assembly is a great way to do this. As a group that has been preparing for this threat for longer than anyone else it likely will be your responsibility to guide any action needed. So make a good assembly agenda, share what you know about the local context, come in with a plan of action and help people clarify their own ideas — but also remain humble and open to changing plans. Once an assembly is over, it’s good to get as many attendees and community members as possible into an alerts-only Signal thread to communicate about the fascists, similar to ICE rapid response groups you may already be in. Encourage people to organize into location-based teams by having people in the same class or dorm group up and make their own preparations. Have those chuds panicking over the fact that four dozen people assembled around them in just a few minutes! Stay Tight, Stay Brave Classic Soviet anti-fascist poster from WWII depicting a Red Army soldier bayonetting a swastika-shaped snake. Before you confront any fascists directly, think about other ways you can subvert them. Do they have jobs or family members you could call? Do people in their neighborhood know what they are doing? Can you prevent them from arriving on campus? Or discourage them from coming back in another way? This might not always work, but it’s worth trying to minimize immediate danger. However, even if you do all this, you might still need to confront them. Confronting fascists doesn’t necessarily mean using violence. I should say clearly: if possible, violence should be minimized. No matter what you do, though, a confrontation will be a confrontation. There is a common but wildly incorrect sentiment that fascists can simply be ignored, mocked or defeated through “expressions of our joy.” Fascists’ end goal is our extermination, and leaving them only mildly annoyed, at best, allows them to gain confidence and grow their group. Therefore, we must take direct action to remove them from our spaces. This shouldn’t scare you. Even if you’re small in numbers or stature, with a good plan and good teamwork you can overcome any foe (yes, we will defeat fascism with the power of friendship!). If it comes down to a direct confrontation, remember to stay tight, as fascists are cowards through and through. They like to target smaller or less coordinated groups or individuals. If you show them that you won’t be pushed around, they will crumble. Stay brave too—don’t let them set the pace of the interaction, and keep them on the back foot. If they don’t feel in control of the situation, they’ll likely flee. You can win against Nazis, fascists, Zionists and all other flavors of chud. All it takes is confidence and preparation. When they come onto your campus, you’ll drive them out. I believe in you. Stay strong comrades, and let them hear: “¡No Pasaran!”
